knowledge_point.title: Finding the General Solution of a Differential Equation Using Integration

question.:question/problem: Find the general solution to the differential equation $f'(x)+8 x=0.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, we rearrange the equation to isolate the derivative term:

$$
\begin{aligned}f'(x) &=- 8 x\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate both sides of the equation with respect to $x,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int f'(x)\,\mathrm{d}x &=\int \left(- 8 x\right)\,\mathrm{d}x \\ f(x) &=-8\int x\,\mathrm{d}x \\ &=-8\left(\frac{x^{2}}{2}\right)+C \\ &=- 4 x^{2}+C\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Solve the differential equation $\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}- 8 e^{2 x}=8 x.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, we rearrange the equation to isolate the derivative term:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x} &=8 e^{2 x}+8 x\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate both sides of the equation with respect to $x,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}\,\mathrm{d}x &=\int \left(8 e^{2 x}+8 x\right)\,\mathrm{d}x \\ y &=8\int e^{2 x}\,\mathrm{d}x+8\int x\,\mathrm{d}x \\ &=8\left(\frac{e^{2 x}}{2}\right)+8\left(\frac{x^{2}}{2}\right)+C \\ &=4 x^{2} + 4 e^{2 x}+C\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Find the general solution to the differential equation $f'(x)=8 \sin{\left(2 x \right)}.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, notice that the derivative term is already isolated on the left:

$$
\begin{aligned}f'(x) &=8 \sin{\left(2 x \right)}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate both sides of the equation with respect to $x,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int f'(x)\,\mathrm{d}x &=\int \left(8 \sin{\left(2 x \right)}\right)\,\mathrm{d}x \\ f(x) &=8\int \sin{\left(2 x \right)}\,\mathrm{d}x \\ &=8\left(- \frac{\cos{\left(2 x \right)}}{2}\right)+C \\ &=- 4 \cos{\left(2 x \right)}+C\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Find the general solution to the differential equation $f'(x)=- \frac{8}{2 x - 2}.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, notice that the derivative term is already isolated on the left:

$$
\begin{aligned}f'(x) &=- \frac{8}{2 x - 2}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate both sides of the equation with respect to $x,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int f'(x)\,\mathrm{d}x &=\int \left(- \frac{8}{2 x - 2}\right)\,\mathrm{d}x \\ f(x) &=-8\int \frac{1}{2 x - 2}\,\mathrm{d}x \\ &=-8\left(\frac{\ln{\left(\left|{2 x - 2}\right| \right)}}{2}\right)+C \\ &=- 4 \ln{\left(\left|{2 x - 2}\right| \right)}+C\end{aligned}
$$

This solution holds on any interval that does not contain $x=1$.

question.:question/problem: Find the general solution to the differential equation $f'(x)- 8 x^{2}=8 x.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, we rearrange the equation to isolate the derivative term:

$$
\begin{aligned}f'(x) &=8 x+8 x^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate both sides of the equation with respect to $x,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int f'(x)\,\mathrm{d}x &=\int \left(8 x+8 x^{2}\right)\,\mathrm{d}x \\ f(x) &=8\int x\,\mathrm{d}x+8\int x^{2}\,\mathrm{d}x \\ &=8\left(\frac{x^{2}}{2}\right)+8\left(\frac{x^{3}}{3}\right)+C \\ &=\frac{8 x^{3}}{3} + 4 x^{2}+C \\ &=\frac{4 x^{2} \left(2 x + 3\right)}{3}+C\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Find the general solution to the differential equation $f'(x)- 8 e^{2 x}=8.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, we rearrange the equation to isolate the derivative term:

$$
\begin{aligned}f'(x) &=8+8 e^{2 x}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate both sides of the equation with respect to $x,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int f'(x)\,\mathrm{d}x &=\int \left(8+8 e^{2 x}\right)\,\mathrm{d}x \\ f(x) &=8\int 1\,\mathrm{d}x+8\int e^{2 x}\,\mathrm{d}x \\ &=8\left(x\right)+8\left(\frac{e^{2 x}}{2}\right)+C \\ &=8 x + 4 e^{2 x}+C\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Find the general solution to the differential equation  ${f}^{′}(x)=\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡4x.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, notice that the derivative term is already isolated on the left:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡4x.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate both sides of the equation with respect to $x,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {f}^{′}(x)\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡4x\,\text{d}x \\ f(x) & =\frac{1}{2}\int \operatorname{sin}⁡4x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(-\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{cos}⁡4x) \\  & =-\frac{1}{8}\operatorname{cos}⁡4x+C.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Find the general solution to the differential equation  ${f}^{′}(x)+6{x}^{2}=4x.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, we rearrange the equation to isolate the derivative term:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =4x-6{x}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate both sides of the equation with respect to $x,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {f}^{′}(x)\,\text{d}x & =\int (4x-6{x}^{2})\text{d}x \\  & =4\int x\,\text{d}x-6\int {x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =4\cdot \frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}-6\cdot \frac{1}{3}{x}^{3} \\  & =2{x}^{2}-2{x}^{3}+C \\  & =2{x}^{2}(1-x)+C.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

question.:question/problem: Find the general solution to the differential equation  ${f}^{′}(x)-6{e}^{-3x}=1.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, we rearrange the equation to isolate the derivative term:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =1+6{e}^{-3x}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate both sides of the equation with respect to $x,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {f}^{′}(x)\,\text{d}x & =\int (1+6{e}^{-3x})\text{d}x \\  & =\int \text{d}x+6\int {e}^{-3x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =x+6(-\frac{1}{3}{e}^{-3x}) \\  & =x-2{e}^{-3x}+C.\end{aligned}
$$
